author: product-requirements-expert
title: Specialty directory lists each specialty with the veterinarians holding it
summary: A read-only page lists every specialty the clinic holds, each by its stored name, with the veterinarians holding it. All specialties appear on the one page. The page is reachable by its address alone.
acceptance_criteria: GET /specialties.html lists every specialty the clinic holds, each by its stored name
each veterinarian holding a specialty is listed under that specialty by first name then last name, for example "Helen Leary"
a veterinarian holding no specialty appears nowhere on the page
a specialty no veterinarian holds is still listed, with no veterinarian under it
every specialty appears on the one page, with no paging and nothing held back for a further page
specialties, and the veterinarians under each, appear in a stable order across repeated requests
when the clinic holds no specialty, the page opens and lists none rather than failing
no navigation entry and no link from another page leads to the page
the page's user-facing wording is present in every supported language, with none fixed into the page (REQ-LANG-002)
the page carries the navigation every page carries (REQ-SYS-001)
non_goals: managing veterinarians or their specialties through the application (NG-2, unchanged by this slice)
a navigation entry or a link from another page to the specialty page
searching or filtering the specialty page (NG-9)
a machine-readable form of the specialty list
notes: No Non-Goals row changed, so no scope_overrides. NG-2 stands: this is read-only presentation. The owner ruled out further product answers, so three open choices were resolved by the narrowest reading and recorded in the PRD Open Questions rather than consulted: (1) an unheld specialty is still listed; (2) any stable order is enough, alphabetical is unconfirmed; (3) a visible entry point is deferred to a possible follow-up request. "No navigation entry" means no entry point TO this page; the page still carries the standard navigation, which REQ-SYS-001 requires of every page. New page wording falls under REQ-LANG-002 and must be translated across every supported bundle.

author: system-design-expert
architectural_fit: The slice stays inside the vet feature package and reuses its existing shape: a Spring Data repository per persisted type, a package-private controller depending on repositories directly, a Thymeleaf page under templates/vets, and the shared layout fragment. One thing is genuinely new. The stored association is unidirectional from Vet to Specialty, so the page inverts it, and no page in the codebase derives its state today. architecture-principles.md admits no business rule in a web controller and states the existing deviation does not extend to new rules, so the inversion and ordering go into an immutable read model in the vet package rather than into VetController. Recorded as ADR 2026-08-11-read-models-for-derived-page-state. Everything else is pattern reuse: SpecialtyRepository mirrors PetTypeRepository (owner package) as the lookup-type repository beside the aggregate one.
integration_points: VetController gains a second HTML route, GET /specialties.html, alongside the existing /vets.html. It takes no request parameter: there is no page parameter, because the page does not page, and no other input.

New SpecialtyRepository extends Repository<Specialty, Integer> with one ordered read method, following VetRepository's narrow interface rather than PetTypeRepository's JpaRepository. NG-2 keeps this read-only, so the write surface stays unexposed.

The veterinarian side reuses VetRepository.findAll(), which is @Cacheable("vets") and eagerly fetches specialties. No new cache and no change to CacheConfiguration. Note that findAll() is today reached only from the /vets route, which Known Defects lists as pending removal; removing that route must keep the method.

The page uses the shared layout fragment with a menu key matching no menu item, so it carries the standard navigation (REQ-SYS-001) while no navigation entry leads to it. Do not add a menu item to fragments/layout.html.

Wording reuses the existing message keys specialties, vets, and none, so no bundle needs a new key. Any key that does prove necessary must be added to messages.properties and to all nine translated bundles, or I18nPropertiesSyncTest fails.

patterns.description: lookup-type repository sitting beside the aggregate repository in the same feature package, returning rows in name order via an explicit query
narrow Spring Data Repository interface exposing only the reads the feature needs; the cached whole-collection read the directory builds on
ordering a persisted association by name at the read boundary rather than relying on stored order; the specialty directory orders both of its levels the same way
page structure: layout fragment with a menu key, an h2 bound to a message key, a Bootstrap table with th:each rows

risks.risk: Grouping veterinarians under specialties inside VetController would add a fresh business rule to a controller, which architecture-principles.md rules out and which the existing recorded deviation does not cover.
risks.mitigation: Put the inversion and both orderings in an immutable SpecialtyDirectory built by a static factory from the two repository results; the controller only reads, delegates, and names the view (see the ADR).

risks.risk: Stable order across repeated requests is an acceptance criterion, and both repository reads return unordered collections by default; the vet cache can also change iteration order.
risks.mitigation: Order specialties by stored name in the repository query, and veterinarians within each specialty by last name, then first name, then identity as a total tiebreak. Order is imposed by the read path, never inherited from the store.

risks.risk: Every specialty on one page with no paging turns an unbounded table into an unbounded response.
risks.mitigation: Accepted for this slice: the specialty list is a small seeded lookup table, and no-paging is the requirement. Flagged here so a future growth in that table is recognized as a design change, not a rendering bug.

risks.risk: Vet.specialties is EAGER over a many-to-many, so a whole-collection findAll() issues a per-veterinarian association fetch.
risks.mitigation: No new exposure: this is the existing load profile of the vet routes, served from the same "vets" cache. Do not add a second cache or a new fetch strategy in this slice.

risks.risk: An empty clinic and a specialty no veterinarian holds are both required to render rather than fail.
risks.mitigation: The read model treats both as ordinary empty collections, never as absent values; the template renders an empty table body and the existing none wording under an unheld specialty.

notes: Autofix audit: no design-doc-autofix records in the log, nothing to audit. Durable-memory writes for this verdict: one ADR (docs/adr/2026-08-11-read-models-for-derived-page-state.md) plus its index row. docs/system-design.md is deliberately untouched. That document is current state only, and SpecialtyRepository, SpecialtyDirectory, and the second route do not exist yet; their Contracts rows, and REQ-VET-003 in the Implements column, land through doc-sync after the code does. Narrow readings taken, matching the PRD Open Questions rather than adding to them: stable order is realized as alphabetical by stored name because that is what the codebase already does for specialties and pet types, and it costs nothing over an arbitrary stable order; no navigation entry and no link is realized as a layout menu key matching no item. The prd-entry lists messages.properties among file_targets; under this design it likely stays unchanged, because reusing the three existing keys avoids nine translations for wording no one has confirmed. file_targets is the starting set, not a contract to touch every file. Test shape: four of the five named behaviors are properties of the read model and are cheapest as unit tests over real Vet and Specialty objects; the route, the one-page rendering, and the navigation belong in VetControllerTests with MockMvc. Splitting them that way is expected, not a deviation from the named tests.

author: security-reviewer
approved_aspects: No injection surface added: SpecialtyRepository.findSpecialties() is a static, parameterless JPQL string ('SELECT specialty FROM Specialty specialty ORDER BY specialty.name') with no concatenation and no request-derived value; the ORDER BY is a fixed literal, not caller input. Meets the injection-into-data-access control in security-principles.md.

No XSS introduced: every user-derived value in templates/vets/specialtyList.html renders through th:text (entry.name, the joined veterinarian names, and the message keys), which keeps Thymeleaf's default escaping on. Swept the whole templates tree for th:utext, th:inline and script-context expressions and found none, so this change does not start a class. #strings.listJoin output is escaped by the enclosing th:text.

No new input boundary: GET /specialties.html takes no request parameter, no path variable and no request body, so there is nothing to validate, no binder to configure, and no mass-assignment or identifier-tampering surface. The lack of an @InitBinder disallow list is correct here rather than an omission.

Least privilege on the new repository: SpecialtyRepository extends Repository<Specialty, Integer> rather than JpaRepository or CrudRepository, exposing exactly one @Transactional(readOnly = true) read. No save, delete, or flush surface reaches the container, so NG-2's read-only stance is enforced by the type, not by convention.

Data exposure is unchanged, not widened: the page re-projects veterinarian names and specialty names that /vets.html and the /vets serialized route already return to any unauthenticated caller. No field beyond first name, last name and specialty name reaches the model; SpecialtyDirectory.Entry carries strings only, so no entity, identifier, or association leaks into the view. Per security-principles.md the absence of authentication is the demonstration's recorded baseline and is not raised as a defect; this change does not make it worse. The absence of a navigation entry is a product decision (PRD open question, 2026-08-11), not a security control, and nothing here depends on the URL staying unguessed.

No secrets: swept the diff for credential-shaped names (token, password, secret, key, credential, passwd, apikey, connection string) — the only 'key' hits are Map.Entry::getKey in the grouping collector and the message keys in the template. No new configuration, no new environment variable, no committed default.

Supply chain unchanged: build.gradle and the Gradle wrapper are untouched by the change set (confirmed via git status and the changeset file list), so no new coordinate, repository, or plugin enters the build. No dependency review was owed and the four checks in system-design.md Adding a New Dependency do not apply to this slice.

No deserialization, file, or process boundary crossed: the change adds no serialization hint, reads no classpath or filesystem resource from a request-derived value, and starts no process. Actuator exposure and CacheConfiguration are untouched, so the management surface is unchanged.

Error handling adds no disclosure: the handler surfaces only DataAccessException from the repository read, which falls through to the existing error page exactly as the /vets.html handler does; no new exception message is constructed and none carries a credential, query text, or connection detail.

author: code-quality-reviewer

findings.description: Entry.veterinarians is typed List<String> and actually holds formatted full names, not Vet objects — the field/parameter name reads as if entry.veterinarians() returns veterinarians. A reader calling entry.veterinarians() and getting strings back has to open the javadoc to learn what it really is. The record parameter, the fullNames() parameter binding site, and the specialtyList.html template all inherit this naming.
findings.fix: Rename the record component (and the local variable it flows from) to veterinarianNames, e.g. `public record Entry(String name, List<String> veterinarianNames)`, and update SpecialtyDirectory.of/fullNames and templates/vets/specialtyList.html's entry.veterinarians references to entry.veterinarianNames.

findings.description: BY_LAST_THEN_FIRST_NAME mixes an explicit typed lambda for the first key (`(Vet vet) -> vet.getLastName()`) with a method reference for the second (`Person::getFirstName`), and imports Person solely to write the second half. Both keys come from the same Vet (which extends Person), so the inconsistency is unmotivated — it reads as if the two halves were written by different rules.
findings.fix: Use method references for both: `Comparator.comparing(Vet::getLastName).thenComparing(Vet::getFirstName)`, dropping the now-unneeded import of org.springframework.samples.petclinic.model.Person.

approved_aspects: SpecialtyDirectory keeps the inversion and both orderings out of VetController, matching the ADR and the Web-controller row in architecture-principles.md

SpecialtyRepository mirrors PetTypeRepository's narrow lookup-repository shape (findSpecialties, ORDER BY name) rather than pulling in JpaRepository's full write surface, consistent with the read-only NG-2 constraint
Both SpecialtyDirectory and Entry are proper immutable records with defensive List.copyOf in their compact constructors
Empty-clinic and unheld-specialty cases are handled as ordinary empty collections, not special-cased or null
./gradlew checkFormat and checkstyleMain both pass clean on the changed files
specialtyList.html reuses the shared layout fragment (UTF-8 meta already there) and existing message keys, matching vetList.html's structure

author: test-reviewer

findings.description: SpecialtyRepository.findSpecialties() is new persistence logic — a JPQL query (`ORDER BY specialty.name`) that is the sole mechanism delivering the 'stable order across repeated requests' acceptance criterion for specialties. No test in the change set exercises it against a real database. SpecialtyDirectoryTests builds SpecialtyDirectory directly from already-ordered in-memory lists, so it never touches the query. VetControllerTests mocks SpecialtyRepository (`given(this.specialties.findSpecialties()).willReturn(...)`), so it never touches the query either. The project's existing pattern for exactly this case is ClinicServiceTests (@DataJpaTest, real H2, seeded via src/main/resources/db/h2/data.sql), which already covers VetRepository/OwnerRepository queries but was not extended to cover SpecialtyRepository. The seed data (`radiology`, `surgery`, `dentistry`, in that non-alphabetical insert order) would make a real test meaningful: a broken or missing ORDER BY would pass every test in this change set today. This is the one piece of real I/O the slice added, and per the brief's Mocking Policy ('Real I/O for integration... Use real files, real filesystem, real test data') and Test Pyramid ('~15% integration, real I/O'), it needs a data-layer test, not just a unit test over a hand-built list and a controller test over a mocked repository.

The specialty ids passed to specialty(3, "anesthesia"), specialty(4, "cardiology"), specialty(5, "dentistry"), specialty(6, "neurology"), and specialty(7, "surgery") are bare mystery literals (Three-Tier Data Naming, Tier 3): they have no bearing on the test's outcome (only the names matter for the stringContainsInOrder assertion) but are not marked as irrelevant via a SOME_/ANY_ prefix or an id-generating anonymous factory, unlike SpecialtyDirectoryTests' own vet()/specialty() helpers which use a shared nextId counter for exactly this reason.
findings.fix: Give the specialty(int, String) factory an overload specialty(String name) that assigns an irrelevant, internally generated id (e.g. a static counter, as SpecialtyDirectoryTests already does), and use it for every specialty in this test except the one bound to RADIOLOGY_ID.

findings.description: Coverage matches the ordering guarantee as the design-block actually narrowed it: theSpecialtyDirectoryShouldOrderVeterinariansByLastThenFirstName exercises the last-name-then-first-name comparator including a genuine tie on last name (two Jenkins), and no test needs to distinguish two veterinarians tied on both names because, as the javadoc states, they render identically regardless of internal order — there is nothing observable to assert. That reasoning holds for a single directory build. It does not, on its own, cover 'stable order across repeated requests' (PRD acceptance criterion) for the tied-name case: stability there additionally depends on Stream.sorted() being a stable sort and on the veterinarian collection arriving in the same encounter order on every call (i.e., on VetRepository.findAll()'s @Cacheable("vets") returning the identical cached list rather than re-querying in a different order). No test in this change set — unit or MockMvc — asserts that two successive calls to the endpoint return byte-identical output. This is not a defect in the tests submitted; it is a gap between the acceptance criterion's literal scope (repeated requests) and what any test here checks (single build/request). Flagging so the design-block's accepted rationale is recorded as covering the single-build case explicitly, or a repeated-request assertion is added if the brief intends otherwise.

approved_aspects: SpecialtyDirectoryTests exercises the read model over real Vet/Specialty objects with zero mocking, matching the brief's mocking policy for a pure domain unit

All four PRD-named unit-test behaviors present and correctly split; the fifth (no-pagination) correctly lands in VetControllerTests where model attributes are observable, matching the design-block's accepted test split
Every Specialty built in SpecialtyDirectoryTests carries an assigned id, avoiding the NPE risk the design-block flagged for SpecialtyDirectory.of's getId()-keyed grouping
BDD naming (the{Subject}Should{Outcome}) followed consistently in all eight new/modified test methods
The no-navigation-link acceptance criterion has a dedicated, correctly targeted assertion (not(containsString("specialties.html")))
AssertJ used throughout SpecialtyDirectoryTests with collection-aware assertions (containsExactly, flatExtracting, tuple); no JUnit assertEquals/assertTrue anywhere in the new tests

risks.risk: The specialty level of the stable-order criterion is not total. SpecialtyRepository.findSpecialties orders by specialty.name alone, and no vendor schema constrains specialties.name unique — all three declare a plain index. Two specialties sharing a name are distinct entries under SpecialtyDirectory.of, which groups on identity, so their relative order is observable on the page and the database may vary it between requests.
risks.mitigation: Make the read-path order total: ORDER BY specialty.name, specialty.id in the JPQL. This does not reverse the identity tiebreak dropped at line 8 for veterinarians — there the tiebreak was unobservable and a null id would have failed for an unsaved instance, while here the order is observable per entry, the sort runs in the database, and specialties reach the query with identity always set.

risks.risk: A future author reads the veterinarian ordering as depending on Stream.sorted() stability or on the vets cache returning a fixed encounter order, and adds a guard against neither.
risks.mitigation: Neither dependency is load-bearing; the reasoning is recorded in notes and the class javadoc already states the tie case. No code change and no test.

notes: Autofix audit: the log holds no design-doc-autofix records, so nothing to audit. No supersedes_record_at: the design guidance is carried forward intact, and setting it would void this round's code-quality and security approvals for a doc sync plus one query token. ||| CLARIFY ANSWER (test-reviewer, line 18, clarify_target system-design-expert). Verdict: record the rationale, do not add a repeated-request assertion. The reviewer names two dependencies for the tied-name case; neither is load-bearing. SpecialtyDirectory sorts veterinarians and only then projects each to a formatted name string. Two veterinarians tied on both names emit identical strings, so any permutation of them yields an identical List<String>. The emitted list is therefore a function of the multiset of names alone — independent of Stream.sorted() being stable and independent of the encounter order @Cacheable(\"vets\") returns. A byte-identity assertion over two successive calls would assert a property guaranteed by construction, and asserting sort stability would test the JDK rather than this code. The single-build coverage the reviewer describes is accepted as covering the veterinarian level of the criterion in full. ||| The clarify did surface one genuine residual the reviewer did not reach: the specialty level, recorded as the first risk above. ||| FOR THE IMPLEMENTER, one code change and no new test beyond the one already required. Do not add a repeated-request or byte-identity test anywhere. ||| Durable-memory writes this dispatch: docs/system-design.md (Contracts rows, Implements columns, Invariants paragraph, provenance banner clause) and one stale clause removed from the ADR's References. docs/prd.md untouched, docs/adr/README.md untouched.

findings.description: Disposition of my prior blocked finding accepted: the test now exercises SpecialtyRepository.findSpecialties() against real H2 seeded from db/h2/data.sql, closing the 'query untested by any real I/O' gap. Residual noted for the record, not reblocking: because src/main/resources/db/h2/schema.sql:21 indexes specialties.name, H2 serves the unordered scan in name order on its own, so deleting the JPQL ORDER BY does not fail this test (implementer-verified, and consistent with reasoning about H2's query planner over an indexed column with no WHERE clause) — only a wrong ORDER BY (e.g. by id) fails it. The test still meaningfully exercises the query against real seeded data and distinguishes 'ordered by name' from 'ordered by id', which is the coverage the brief's Mocking Policy asks for; a mutation-proof-against-missing-ORDER-BY test would require either changing the shared schema (out of this slice, correctly declined) or forcing a query plan that bypasses the index, neither of which is reasonable in an integration test. Accepting as designed; the in-test comment already documents the limitation for the next reader, which is the right way to carry a known test-boundary forward.

author: change-grader

blast_radius.note: Eleven files in one module, all additive: a new route, a new read model, a new narrow repository, a new template, and doc rows. The only edit to existing production code is VetController's constructor gaining a second injected repository, and the existing /vets.html and /vets routes are untouched; no sensitive path, no schema, no build file, no message bundle (the template reuses four keys that already exist in all eleven languages).

semantic_surprise.note: Read all 30 hunks: the inversion groups veterinarians by specialty id and falls back to an empty list, so a specialty nobody holds still yields an entry, matching the stated narrowest reading; the record copies both lists defensively, the template escapes every database-derived string through th:text, and Vet.specialties is EAGER so the detached, vet-cache-held entities render outside a transaction safely. The one non-obvious point is deliberate and documented: veterinarians sort by last name then first name while rendering first-name-first, so listing Alan Jenkins, Sharon Jenkins, Helen Leary is correct rather than mis-sorted.

test_adequacy.note: The read model and the controller are covered well - six unit tests over real Vet and Specialty objects, three MockMvc tests asserting rendered order, absence of a vet holding no specialty, absence of paging attributes, and absence of a self-link - but the one guarantee this slice pushed into the database survives mutation: the implementer verified that deleting ORDER BY specialty.name from findSpecialties leaves shouldListEverySpecialtyInNameOrder green, because schema.sql:21 indexes specialties.name and H2 serves the scan sorted unaided. Only a wrong ORDER BY fails it, so the specialty-level ordering promise rests on one database's query plan rather than on a test.

reviewer_hedging.note: All four dispatched reviewers approved, but the test-reviewer's approval carries a clarify finding under bar_clause tested-as-spec that records the surviving ORDER BY mutation and routes it to the system-design-expert rather than closing it; that is approval with a live caveat, not a clean approval. Worth weighing alongside the history: the first review round produced three changes_requested verdicts including a critical doc-reviewer block, all resolved on re-review.

scope_deviation.note: The diff matches the PRD's ten acceptance criteria and the design block's named paths, with no build retries and no consultations. Two recorded deltas, both benign: the planned SpecialtyRepositoryTests.java landed as a test inside ClinicServiceTests instead, following the project's existing real-I/O repository pattern, and the single design revision was bookkeeping - covering the ADR index row, then syncing system-design.md after a review finding - rather than a re-triage. The three unanswered product questions are recorded as open questions in the PRD, not silently decided.

rationale: The database ordering promise is exercised only by a DataJpaTest that H2's specialties_name index passes even with the ORDER BY deleted, so specialty order rests on one engine's query plan; the test-reviewer approved that residual rather than closing it.
